steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Conformity is changing your behaviour or beliefs to fit in with a group. Internalisation: genuinely accepting group norms (deep, lasting change). Identification: adopting group behaviour to gain membership. Compliance: going along publicly but not privately changing.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Asch's (1951) line conformity experiment: 75% of participants conformed at least once, giving a clearly wrong answer. Conformity increased with group size (up to 3) and unanimity, but decreased with a dissenting partner.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Milgram's (1963) obedience study: 65% of participants delivered the maximum 450V shock when instructed by an authority figure. Obedience increased with proximity of authority, legitimacy of the institution, and uniform.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Zimbardo's (1973) Stanford Prison Experiment: participants assigned as guards became abusive; prisoners became passive and distressed. The study showed how social roles can alter behaviour dramatically. Terminated after 6 days.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe Asch's conformity experiment and evaluate its methodology. | Explain why people obey authority, referring to Milgram's research. | Evaluate the ethical issues in Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Conformity types: IIC - Internalisation (deepest), Identification (middle), Compliance (shallowest). Asch = conformity (peer pressure). Milgram = obedience (authority). Zimbardo = social roles. Dissenting partner reduces conformity dramatically - one person standing up makes it easier for others.
